analysis.one_liner: Replaces Affordable Care Act coverage rules with flat tax credits, health savings accounts, and skinnier insurance plans.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote, and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the requirement that large employers offer affordable health coverage, drop the federal requirement that plans cover a set of essential health benefits or preventive care at no cost, and let states allow plans with annual benefit caps. It would replace Affordable Care Act premium subsidies with a flat tax credit of roughly $2,500 per adult and $1,500 per child usable only for plans that do not cover abortion beyond narrow exceptions, create tax-advantaged 'Roth' health savings accounts, and convert federal Medicaid payments into a capped, per-beneficiary system. The bill was referred to three committees in March 2022 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers gain by no longer facing penalties for not offering affordable coverage and by shedding premium-reporting paperwork. Health insurers gain the flexibility to sell plans without required benefits or preventive-care coverage, and would pick up new customers through state default enrollment. Households with cash on hand gain from Roth health savings accounts and a flat credit that does not phase out at higher incomes the way the current subsidies do. Uninsured people buying coverage gain the new tax credit, including some higher earners who get nothing under current law.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an advanceable, refundable health insurance tax credit of about $2,500 per adult and $1,500 per child per year, usable toward premiums and health savings account contributions.
Repeals the Affordable Care Act employer mandate and the related employer reporting requirements, removing potential penalties for businesses with 50 or more full-time workers.
Establishes Roth health savings accounts that can pay premiums, long-term care coverage, and even concierge-medicine fees, with tax-free withdrawals for medical expenses.
Keeps several current protections: no denial or pricing based on pre-existing conditions, guaranteed renewability, guaranteed availability of coverage, and dependent coverage through age 26.

Lets states enroll uninsured residents in a default high-deductible plan with an easy opt-out, apply unused tax credits to indigent care, and offer Medicaid enrollees a private plan plus a deposit of the credit difference into a health savings account.

analysis.who_pays: People with ongoing or expensive health needs bear the biggest cost, since plans would no longer have to cover essential health benefits or preventive care at no cost and could impose annual caps. Adults covered by Medicaid expansion would face capped federal funding. The Treasury pays for the new tax credit. Anyone who lets coverage lapse pays a 20% premium surcharge for each year without coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with health needs and Medicaid expansion adults

drawbacks.text: Health plans would no longer be required to cover preventive care at no cost or include the Affordable Care Act's essential health benefits, so plans could strip coverage for things like maternity care, mental health, or prescription drugs.

Plans with annual benefit caps would be allowed, and exchanges would have to offer them for a state's residents to qualify for subsidies; someone who hits the cap is shielded from debt beyond the bankruptcy value of their property, but providers may refuse further care without payment guaranteed in advance.
People who go without coverage for a year or more would face a 20% premium surcharge for each consecutive year without coverage when they try to enroll again.

Federal Medicaid payments would become capped, per-beneficiary amounts, states would have to contribute their own share, and federal money could not generally be used for adults above 100% of the poverty line except for children, pregnant women, and certain other groups.

The new tax credit can only go toward plans that exclude abortion coverage except in cases of rape, incest, or danger to the mother's life, and it is capped at what the household actually pays in premiums and account contributions, so people who cannot pay up front capture less of it. The medical expense deduction would also be repealed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The flat credit is a real benefit for uninsured people buying their own coverage, especially moderate and higher earners who currently get no subsidy, and repealing the employer mandate reduces a compliance burden on businesses. But the trade is stark for anyone who actually gets sick: mandated benefits, free preventive care, and the ban on annual caps would disappear, a coverage-gap surcharge would punish the uninsured, and Medicaid funding would be capped. Households with chronic conditions or lower incomes would likely pay substantially more out of pocket, while the gains flow disproportionately to employers, insurers, and households with cash to put into savings accounts. It is a broad deregulation of the insurance market with a smaller, differently-targeted subsidy bolted on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill on March 28, 2022, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees.
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No member of either party cosponsored the bill.
No committee took it up, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so people who rely on Affordable Care Act protections and on Medicaid avoided the proposed rollbacks, while employers and insurers kept operating under current law rather than gaining the added flexibility.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People on ACA plans and Medicaid

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored the bill and no Democrat cosponsored, and since no vote was ever held the record shows no partisan split beyond that.

industries.note: Insurers could sell plans without required benefits, without no-cost preventive care, and with annual benefit caps, and states could default-enroll uninsured residents into high-deductible plans, expanding their customer base with skinnier products. The gain comes from customers receiving less coverage per dollar.

The bill repeals the Affordable Care Act employer mandate penalties and the related premium reporting, cutting a cost and compliance burden. Some workers could end up with no employer coverage as a result.
Roth health savings accounts would create a new class of accounts that banks and insurers administer for fees. The tax advantages accrue mainly to households with spare cash to contribute.

Physicians could collect prepaid monthly access fees paid from health savings accounts, and such arrangements would be exempt from health-insurance regulation. Access depends on paying recurring fees up front.

Converting Medicaid payments to capped per-beneficiary amounts with required state shares would shrink federal funding that supports hospitals serving low-income patients, though the bill channels a share of unused tax credits to indigent care and disproportionate-share payments.
